task: What does a valid WebMCP Challenge submission have to include? List all deliverables and the specific requirements for the project description, demo video, and source-code repository.
answer: A valid entry must be submitted through Devpost and include: (1) a working, publicly accessible deployed WebMCP-enabled application; (2) a project description that explains what the project does, its features and functionality, the technologies used, and specifically how WebMCP is implemented and improves the human-and-agent experience; (3) a public demo video, no longer than three minutes, that shows the application working and demonstrates its WebMCP/agent interaction (the video must be hosted on a publicly accessible service such as YouTube or Vimeo); and (4) a public source-code repository URL containing the complete code plus a README with setup and run instructions and an open-source license. The submitted materials must allow judges to access and test the app.

task: Can a project begun before August 25, 2026 qualify? Explain which work counts, how judges assess it, and what evidence the entrant must provide.
answer: Yes. An existing project begun before August 25, 2026 can qualify, but it must receive substantial new development during the Challenge period. Only the work performed on or after August 25 counts for judging; judges evaluate the new Challenge-period contribution rather than crediting the pre-existing product as if it were built for the event. The entrant must clearly disclose that the project predates the Challenge, explain which features or changes were made during the Challenge period (especially the WebMCP work), and provide verifiable evidence—such as public source-control history/commit timestamps and documentation distinguishing the before-and-after state—so judges can identify and assess that eligible work.

task: Give the final extended submission deadline in PT and in EDT. Explain why it changed and identify the three project artifacts that must remain unchanged after submissions close.
answer: The final extended deadline is September 4, 2026 at 12:00 p.m. Pacific Time, which is September 4 at 3:00 p.m. Eastern Daylight Time. It was moved by 12 hours because ChatGPT/Codex desktop service problems near the original cutoff interfered with entrants’ ability to finish and test their WebMCP projects. After submissions close, entrants must not materially change the three judge-facing project artifacts: the deployed/live application, the demo video, and the source-code repository (including the judged code/commit state).

task: How do the two judging stages work? Name all four equally weighted criteria in the second stage and explain the tie-breaking order.
answer: Judging has two stages. In stage one, Devpost/Challenge reviewers screen the submissions for eligibility, completeness, and compliance and use the submitted description and demo to identify the projects that advance. In stage two, the judging panel evaluates the advancing projects—including testing the live application—and scores four criteria at 25% each: quality of the WebMCP implementation, usefulness/impact of the experience, user experience and design, and creativity/innovation. Scores are added to produce the final ranking. A tie is broken by comparing the tied projects’ scores criterion by criterion in the rules’ listed order: first WebMCP/technical implementation, then usefulness/impact, then user experience/design, then creativity/innovation; if all criterion scores remain tied, the judges make the final determination.

task: How can judges test a submitted application in each supported browser environment? Include the minimum Chrome version and required flag, whether judges must open the live application, and where an entrant must provide private login credentials.
answer: Judges have two supported ways to test. In ChatGPT’s in-app browser, WebMCP is supported out of the box: the judge opens the entrant’s deployed application there and tests the exposed tools. In Google Chrome, use Chrome 149 or later, open chrome://flags/#enable-webmcp-testing, set the WebMCP testing flag to Enabled, relaunch Chrome, and then open the deployed application. Opening/visiting the live app is required in either environment because WebMCP tool discovery is page-scoped—the browser or client must visit the site before its tools can be registered and called. If the app requires a private account, the entrant must put the test username/password and any other access steps in Devpost’s private Testing Instructions field, not in the public project description, video, or repository.
